clinicalPearls: A neutrophilic scarring alopecia characterised by recurrent crops of follicular pustules and expanding patches of scarring hair loss, usually on the vertex and occiput
The hallmark is tufted folliculitis, in which several hairs emerge from a single dilated follicular opening within scarred skin, sometimes described as doll's hair
Perifollicular erythema, pustules, crusting and haemorrhagic crusts accompany active disease, which is often painful or itchy
Staphylococcus aureus is frequently isolated and is thought to drive an abnormal host inflammatory response, though the condition is not a simple infection
Loss of follicular ostia confirms the scarring nature, and the disease progresses in a relapsing and remitting fashion
Diagnosis is clinical, supported by trichoscopy showing tufting and perifollicular pustules with an epidermal starburst pattern, and by biopsy, while swabs guide antibacterial choice
Management combines prolonged anti-inflammatory antibiotic-class therapy, often targeting staphylococci, with topical or intralesional corticosteroids and antiseptics to control flares
reference.pathophysiology: Folliculitis decalvans is a primary neutrophilic cicatricial alopecia in which an exaggerated host immune response, frequently associated with Staphylococcus aureus colonisation and possibly a superantigen effect, produces suppurative folliculitis. Sustained neutrophilic inflammation destroys the follicular epithelium and surrounding tissue, and clustering of retained follicles within a shared dilated ostium produces the characteristic tufts. Progressive perifollicular fibrosis leads to permanent follicular loss.
additionalDifferentials: Dissecting cellulitis of the scalp, with boggy nodules, sinuses and the follicular occlusion tetrad
Lichen planopilaris and other lymphocytic scarring alopecias
additionalInvestigations: Bacterial swab and culture, commonly growing Staphylococcus aureus, including assessment of nasal carriage
Trichoscopy showing tufting, perifollicular pustules and an epidermal starburst pattern
Scalp biopsy demonstrating neutrophilic perifollicular inflammation and fibrosis
Consideration of underlying immunosuppression in severe or atypical disease
Monitoring for antibiotic resistance during prolonged courses of therapy
redFlags: Rapidly progressive or widespread scarring with intractable pain
Features overlapping dissecting cellulitis or hidradenitis suggesting follicular occlusion disease
Systemic upset or signs of deep infection
Failure to respond, prompting reassessment for resistant organisms or an alternative diagnosis
reference.prognosis: The condition is chronic and relapsing; treatment can suppress inflammation and limit spread but cannot restore hair in scarred areas, and prolonged or repeated courses of therapy are often required.
pitfalls: Treating as simple bacterial folliculitis with short antibiotic courses, leading to relapse
Failing to recognise tufting as the diagnostic clue
Not addressing staphylococcal carriage, allowing recurrence
Overlooking overlap with other follicular occlusion disorders
management: Suppress the neutrophilic folliculitis with prolonged antistaphylococcal antibiotics, using combination therapy such as rifampicin with clindamycin for refractory disease
Reduce Staphylococcus aureus load with topical antiseptic washes and intranasal decolonisation, for example with mupirocin, of the patient and household carriers
Control inflammation with topical or intralesional corticosteroids and topical antibacterials during flares
For disease refractory to antibiotics, consider oral isotretinoin, dapsone or a TNF-alpha inhibitor biologic
Provide symptomatic relief for the pain and pruritus of active lesions
Guide antibacterial choice by swab and culture and monitor for emerging resistance during prolonged courses
Counsel that treatment suppresses activity but cannot regrow hair in scarred areas, and refer to dermatology for ongoing specialist care
